client: Lately, I've been really struggling with work. My manager just assigned me this huge project with an impossible deadline, and half my team is out on leave. I feel like I'm drowning, but when I try to talk to my boss about it, she just says "you've got this" and moves on. I don't know if therapy can really help when the problem is just too much work.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling overwhelmed and unheard in this situation - that's completely understandable when facing such heavy demands without adequate support. I'm curious, when you say you feel like you're drowning, what thoughts come up for you in those moments?

client: My mind just races with worst-case scenarios - I think "I'm going to fail spectacularly," or "Everyone will see I'm not actually competent." I know logically that's probably not true, but in the moment it feels so real and terrifying. And then I feel guilty for not being able to handle it like I "should" be able to.
therapist: Those thoughts of failure and self-doubt must feel incredibly intense and consuming when they arise, especially paired with that sense of guilt about not meeting expectations. I wonder if we could explore together how these thoughts might be influencing your emotions and actions - when those worries come up, how do you typically respond to them?

client: Usually, I just try to push through and work even harder, staying up late and skipping breaks to get everything done. But honestly, that just makes me feel more exhausted and anxious. I know it's probably not the best approach, but I don't know what else to do when I feel like everything's piling up.
therapist: It sounds like your approach of pushing through has become a cycle that's actually adding to your stress and exhaustion rather than helping. I'm curious - when you think about taking breaks or setting boundaries, what thoughts or fears come up for you?

client: I worry that if I take breaks or try to set boundaries, I'll fall even further behind and let everyone down. There's this nagging voice in my head saying "If you're not working every possible minute, you're being lazy." I know that's probably not healthy, but it feels impossible to ignore when the stakes feel so high.
therapist: It sounds like that inner voice is putting a lot of pressure on you and creating a sense of guilt whenever you consider taking care of yourself. I wonder if we could explore together how this belief about needing to work every minute might be impacting your overall well-being and productivity?

client: I guess I know logically that working non-stop isn't sustainable, but it's hard to see another way when the workload feels so crushing. Even thinking about taking breaks makes me feel anxious and guilty. I'm worried that if I try to set boundaries, my boss will think I'm not committed enough or that I can't handle my job.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between recognizing the need for balance and fearing the consequences of setting boundaries - that must feel really stuck and stressful. I wonder if we could explore together how this cycle of overworking might actually be affecting your ability to perform well, and whether there might be small, manageable ways to introduce balance?

client: I guess I can see that constantly pushing myself isn't sustainable, but the idea of trying to introduce balance feels overwhelming right now. Even small breaks make me anxious because I keep thinking about all the work I "should" be doing instead. I'm worried that if I try to change anything, I'll just fall even further behind.
therapist: It sounds like the thought of taking breaks brings up a lot of anxiety for you, even though you recognize the need for balance - that's such a challenging place to be in. I wonder if we could explore together what might be a small, manageable first step towards introducing balance that feels less overwhelming for you?

client: I guess taking a short break might be possible, but I worry that even a few minutes away from work will make me fall behind. It's hard to imagine how taking breaks could actually help me get more done when I already feel so pressed for time. Maybe there's something small I could try, but I'm not sure where to start without feeling guilty about it.
therapist: It's great that you're open to considering small breaks - that's a meaningful first step towards finding balance. Let's explore together what might be a manageable starting point - perhaps a brief pause or a moment of mindfulness that feels less overwhelming? How could you approach taking breaks in a way that feels more supportive and less guilt-inducing?

client: I guess I could try taking a short break, but I'm worried I'll just spend the whole time thinking about all the work I need to do. Mindfulness sounds nice in theory, but when I've tried it before, I just feel more anxious because I can't stop thinking about my deadlines. It's hard to imagine how taking breaks could actually help me get more done when I already feel so pressed for time.
therapist: It sounds like even the thought of taking a break brings up worries and anxiety for you, which makes it hard to see the potential benefits. Let's explore together what might make breaks feel more manageable and productive for you - perhaps starting with a just few moments where you focus on something simple, like deep breathing or a quick stretch? How could you approach taking breaks in a way that feels less overwhelming and more supportive?

client: I guess I could try taking a few moments to stretch or breathe, but I'm worried I'll just feel guilty about not using that time to work. It's hard to believe that such a small thing could make a difference when I'm so overwhelmed. Part of me feels like I need to keep pushing through, even though I know it's not sustainable.
therapist: It's understandable that even small breaks might feel challenging when you're carrying such a heavy workload and feeling overwhelmed. Let's explore together what might make taking short breaks feel more manageable and supportive for you - perhaps framing them as a way to recharge and improve focus, rather than time away from work? How could you approach taking breaks in a way that feels less guilt-inducing and more productive?

client: I guess framing breaks as a way to recharge makes some sense, but it's hard to believe that a few minutes could really help when I have so much to do. Part of me feels like I'm just wasting time when I could be working, even though I know I'm not at my best when I'm exhausted. It's frustrating because I want to feel better, but it feels like there's no good solution right now.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between recognizing the need to recharge and feeling like breaks aren't productive enough when there's so much to do - that must feel really frustrating and stuck. I wonder if we could explore together how taking small breaks might actually help you be more efficient and focused, rather than seeing them as time away from work? How could you approach taking breaks in a way that feels more supportive and productive for you?
